report:
## Report: Does Vitamin C Prevent Colds?

The evidence does **not fully support "yes."** The most rigorous evidence—a Cochrane systematic review of 29 trials (>11,000 participants)—found that regular vitamin C supplementation (≥200 mg/day) **does not reduce the incidence of colds** in the general population (risk ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.94–1.00) (Cochrane Library, https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD000980.pub4/full; PMC, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152/).

There is one notable exception: in five trials involving people under brief, extreme physical stress—marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers in subarctic conditions—regular vitamin C supplementation **cut cold risk roughly in half**. This suggests physical/environmental stress may deplete vitamin C status enough that supplementation helps in that specific context, but this doesn't generalize to ordinary people.

For the average person, vitamin C's main benefit is modest, not preventive: it **shortens cold duration by about 8–10%** (roughly one day off a week-long cold) and may reduce symptom severity by around 15%, based on the Cochrane review and a 2023 meta-analysis (BMC Public Health, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12889-023-17229-8). Starting vitamin C only after symptoms begin shows no benefit.

The Cochrane authors explicitly concluded: "the failure of vitamin C supplementation to reduce the incidence of colds in the general population indicates that routine vitamin C supplementation is not justified" (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782/).

**Bottom line:** Regular vitamin C does not prevent colds for most people—it may slightly shorten and lessen their severity, and it substantially helps only those under intense physical exertion/cold-stress conditions.
